children.value: Every analysis in this cookbook starts from a bathymetry grid stored as a GeoTIFF file. Before we can compute terrain derivatives or map seabed features, we need to read that file into Python, understand how its pixels relate to real-world positions, and display it. The library that does this is

This notebook is a practical introduction to rasterio. It covers opening a raster, reading its metadata, pulling the pixel values into a NumPy array, and converting between pixel and map coordinates. For visualization it then hands off to the modern raster stack,
, so you never have to hand-write terrain math.
What a georeferenced raster is: an array plus a coordinate reference system and an affine transform.
Opening a dataset and inspecting its metadata.
Reading band values into a NumPy array, including nodata handling.
Converting between pixel indices and map coordinates.

A reusable function for loading and visualizing bathymetric geotiffs.
Rasters carry a CRS and a transform

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as mticker

import rasterio

# rioxarray registers the .rio accessor on xarray objects when imported
import rioxarray
from xrspatial import hillshade

# Tick formatter without scientific notation
formatter = mticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, pos: f"{int(x):,}")

A raster is a regular grid of cells, or pixels, where each cell holds a value. A bathymetry raster holds a water-depth value in every cell. On its own, that grid is just a 2D array of numbers. What makes it a
raster, and not an ordinary image, is two extra pieces of information:
(CRS) that says which place on Earth the grid covers and in what units.
that maps each cell’s (row, column) position to a real-world (x, y) coordinate.
A raster can also hold several

, which are stacked grids of the same size. A satellite image might have red, green, and blue bands; our bathymetry files have a single band. rasterio gives you access to all three parts: the array, the CRS, and the transform.

returns a dataset object. Opening a file does not read the pixel values; it reads only the header, so it is cheap even for very large rasters. We will use the Gifford Canyon bathymetry that ships with this cookbook.
In scripts, open a dataset inside a
block so the file is closed automatically. Here we keep the handle open across several cells for interactive exploration, then close it explicitly at the end.
The dataset object exposes the georeferencing as plain attributes. These are the values you will reach for most often.

print("CRS         :", dataset.crs)
print("Dimensions  :", dataset.width, "x", dataset.height, "(cols x rows)")
print("Band count  :", dataset.count)
print("Data types  :", dataset.dtypes)
print("Nodata value:", dataset.nodata)
print("Bounds      :", dataset.bounds)
print("Resolution  :", dataset.res)
print()
print("Affine transform:")
print(dataset.transform)

children.value: The CRS tells you the map projection and units (metres, here). The resolution is the size of one cell in those units. The transform is the affine matrix that ties pixels to coordinates; we use it in a moment.
For convenience, the whole georeferencing header is available as a single dictionary, the dataset
. This is exactly what you pass back to rasterio when writing a new file.

print("shape:", band1.shape)
print("dtype:", band1.dtype)

children.value: The affine transform is what separates a georeferenced raster from a plain image. It converts a (row, column) pixel index into an (x, y) map coordinate. rasterio wraps this in two convenience methods so you rarely touch the matrix directly:
goes from pixel to map, and

# Pixel (row, col) -> map (x, y)
row, col = 200, 300
x, y = dataset.xy(row, col)
print(f"pixel (row={row}, col={col}) -> map (x={x:.1f}, y={y:.1f})")

# Map (x, y) -> pixel (row, col)
r, c = dataset.index(x, y)
print(f"map (x={x:.1f}, y={y:.1f}) -> pixel (row={r}, col={c})")
applies its inverse. The helper methods also account for whether a coordinate refers to a cell’s centre or corner, which is easy to get wrong by hand.

children.value: Because the array is labelled with
coordinates, a map-aware plot with a colorbar is a single method call.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7), constrained_layout=True)
bathy.plot(ax=ax, cmap="viridis", cbar_kwargs={"label": "Depth (m)"})
ax.set_title("Gifford bathymetry")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
A flat color map hides subtle relief. A
simulates illumination from a low sun, which makes ridges and channels pop out.
computes it directly from the DataArray, deriving slope and aspect internally, so we do not write any gradient math.
is the compass direction of the light source and
is its height above the horizon.

follows the GDAL convention and divides the terrain slope by the true cell size, so the shading is computed in real-world units. On the seafloor the horizontal cell size (50 m here) dwarfs the change in depth from one cell to the next, so the real slopes are gentle and a raw hillshade comes out almost flat. The fix is
: multiply the elevation by a factor before shading, which steepens the apparent slopes and brings the relief back. This is the same idea as
argument. Larger values give more dramatic relief at the cost of physical accuracy, so treat it as a display choice and tune it by eye.

# scale the depth before shading to bring out the gentle seafloor relief
vert_exag = 5
shaded = hillshade(bathy * vert_exag, azimuth=45, angle_altitude=45)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7), constrained_layout=True)
shaded.plot(ax=ax, cmap="gray", add_colorbar=False)
ax.set_title(f"Gifford hillshade (xarray-spatial, vert_exag={vert_exag})")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
plt.show()
Color-shaded relief by overlaying the hillshade

children.label: Color-shaded relief by overlaying the hillshade

children.value: The most readable view combines the depth colormap with the shaded relief. Because the hillshade from the previous cell is itself a labelled DataArray, already vertically exaggerated, we can draw it as a second layer on the same axes: plot the depth in color, then plot the hillshade in grayscale on top with a partial
so the colors show through. The dark and light bands of the hillshade then sculpt the flat colormap into relief. Both layers share the same
coordinates, so they register exactly with no manual extents.
lets more color through; a higher

We built the color-shaded relief in two explicit steps: compute the hillshade as reusable data with
, then overlay it on the colormap with
. Keeping the hillshade as its own DataArray is what makes this possible, and it also lets you save it as a raster or scale the computation across large Dask-backed arrays.
solves the same problem a different way. Its
method computes a hillshade internally and blends it with a colormap in a single call, returning a ready-made RGB image:

from matplotlib.colors import LightSource

ls = LightSource(azdeg=60, altdeg=45)
rgb = ls.shade(bathy.values, cmap=plt.cm.viridis, vert_exag=50, blend_mode="soft")
The trade-off is that the hillshade stays hidden inside the call, and you manage the map extent and colorbar yourself when drawing the result with
. The overlay approach above keeps each layer separate and plots in map coordinates for free.

The same three steps, load, shade, and plot, apply to any single-band bathymetry raster. We wrap them in one function, using the hillshade overlay for the relief, and apply it to a second survey, Point Cloates.

def plot_shaded_relief(path, title, azimuth=315, altitude=45,
                       vert_exag=5, alpha=0.45, cmap="viridis"):
    """Load a single-band raster with rioxarray and plot color-shaded relief
    by overlaying a semi-transparent, vertically exaggerated hillshade on the
    depth colormap."""
    da = rioxarray.open_rasterio(path, masked=True).squeeze()
    # exaggerate the vertical relief so the gentle seafloor slopes shade well
    shaded = hillshade(da * vert_exag, azimuth=azimuth, angle_altitude=altitude)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7), constrained_layout=True)
    da.plot(ax=ax, cmap=cmap, cbar_kwargs={"label": "Depth (m)"})
    shaded.plot(ax=ax, cmap="gray", alpha=alpha, add_colorbar=False)

    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("Easting (m)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Northing (m)")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(formatter)
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(formatter)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    return da

rasterio is the workhorse for reading and writing georeferenced grids. A raster is an array paired with a CRS and an affine transform: the array holds the values, the CRS says where on Earth they sit, and the transform ties pixels to coordinates. You open a file with
, inspect its metadata through attributes like
, and pull band values into NumPy with
methods convert between pixels and map coordinates. For visualization, loading the file with
gives a labelled, CRS-aware array that plots in map coordinates.
turns it into a hillshade with no hand-written terrain math, and because that hillshade is itself a DataArray we overlay it on the depth colormap with a partial
is an alternative that blends the hillshade into the colormap internally in one call.
